# Aedan - Lament of Savior - Prologue

> *"The songs of the gods remember no savior—only survivors."*

---

**Sing, O Muse, for none but us remember—**  
Of Hope, that beguiled its bearer.
Of Mercy, that misled its keeper.
Of Faith, that reason failed to conquer. 
Of the burden no soul should bear.  
Of the boy whom fate had torn asunder.
Sing, at last, of [[Aedan]]—  
and of the tragedy that bore his name.

I write these words in the names of the Olds,  
Who stood powerless when they were needed most.
This is the story of a boy whom I held as the measure of my own duty.  
Whose honor saved the future of children yet unborn.  
Yet, none remembers his name.

Bear with me, for the orthodox ways are all I have ever known.  
Therefore, I shall begin as countless tales have begun before.

Long, long ago, there was once a boy named [[Aedan]].

Though but five summers had passed over his head, 
he walked as one already entrusted with the fate of kingdoms. 
Such is the privilege of childhood, where the world bends willingly before imagination.

Before him loomed an ancient terror.

Its countless limbs stretched toward the heavens. 
Its breath stirred every leaf upon the wind, 
and its voice whispered through the branches in a tongue no mortal ought to know.
Around it lay broken boughs like fallen spears, while scattered leaves danced through the air as though an unseen host had answered its call.

The young hero tightened his grip upon his sword.

"Yield!" he cried. "Your darkness ends today!"

The ancient thing answered only with the groaning of wood and the restless sigh of leaves.

Undaunted, [[Aedan]] charged.

He cleaved through storms of emerald blades. 
Spears rained from every side.
The earth itself seemed to rise against him, 
yet the child would not retreat. 
With every swing he drove the darkness back, 
until at last he stood before its monstrous heart.

"This shall be your end!" shouted by the brave hero.

Yet every hero, no matter how valiant, is strengthened by faithful companions.

Fighting alongside the young hero was a girl of golden hair and emerald eyes.  
She bore a spirit brighter than most children of her age, though one might have guessed as much from the simple fact that she charged beside [[Aedan]] without the slightest hesitation.  
**[[Aine]]** was the name by which she was known.

Behind a broad stone sat a timid-looking boy, his short curls the color of chestnuts and his eyes as blue as the summer sky. A little branch rested forgotten across his lap, for he seemed far more content to watch the battle than to join it.  
**[[Cian]]** was his name.

Thus were the three seldom found apart, each unlike the others, yet together as close as childhood could make them.

Looking back upon those days, I cannot help but think they were the happiest company they would ever know.

"Aedan! Aine! Cian!"

The warm, patient voice carried across the little clearing.

In an instant, the battlefield dissolved.

The dreadful monster became an old oak whose branches swayed lazily beneath the afternoon sun. The swords of the young heroes were no more than crooked sticks, while the faithful sentinel behind his rock clutched nothing grander than a fallen branch. What moments ago had been an epic battle was simply a handful of children, their imaginations breathing life into an ordinary woodland.

"Come," Enna called again. "Your meal is getting cold."

Her name was [[Enna]].

To [[Aedan]], [[Aine]], and [[Cian]], she was sister and mother alike. 
He had never known the faces of those who had brought him into the world. 
Whatever love a child ought to receive from his parents had found its way to him through her gentle hands instead. 
Of course she were the one closest to them

She was all the family they had ever known. And all they would've wanted
And to a kids of five years, she was the whole world.

Though only 13 on the age, [[Enna]] proved to be very mature.
May this by the sole responsibility she bear or by her individuality itself no one would have guess.
She were also the orphan bereft of her parents.
Who to be blamed if not the natural disaster that can occur quiet often.

[[Enna]] turned and disappeared into the little house before the boy could answer. 
She had long since learned that calling twice was unnecessary.
If Aedan did not come at once, it was only because a hero could never be seen abandoning a battlefield in haste.

Aedan remained before the old oak for a moment longer.

He planted his crooked sword into the earth.

"You fought well," he said with all the solemnity of a seasoned warrior. "Tomorrow, we shall finish this."

The ancient foe answered only with the rustling of its leaves.

Satisfied, he turned.

Aine had already begun walking toward the little house.

"You're slow," she called over her shoulder.

"Heroes never flee the battlefield."

"Heroes also don't miss lunch."

Cian quietly stepped out from behind his rock and dusted the dirt from his clothes.

"...I hope there's still bread."

"There won't be if Aine gets there first," Aedan answered.

"I heard that!" Aine shouted.

She immediately broke into a run.

Aedan gave chase.

Cian sighed and followed after them at his own careful pace.

The four gathered around the little table, their wooden swords left forgotten by the door

Aedan puffed out his chest.

"The monster won't trouble the village again."

Enna smiled as she placed another bowl upon the table.

"How fortunate."

She paused.

"Now be just as brave against your vegetables."

The little table was filled with laughter.

Looking back upon that afternoon, I cannot think of a day more peaceful than that.
...Or perhaps I can no longer remember it clearly.
Let us simply agree it was a peaceful day.

The days that followed differed little from one another.

Each morning the little household divided its chores as it always had. Aine and Cian would gather fallen branches from the woods, while Enna made her familiar walk to the village well, returning with two heavy buckets balanced across her shoulders.

So it had always been.

Until one morning.

Enna had scarcely reached for the buckets when Aedan spoke.

"Enna."

She looked over.

"I'll come with you today."

She smiled.

"And leave Aine and Cian to gather all the firewood by themselves?"

Before Aedan could answer, Aine folded her arms.

"We talked about it."

Enna blinked.

"You... talked about it?"

Aine nodded matter-of-factly.

"You always carry both buckets."

"...That's your job."

"It doesn't have to be."

Enna looked toward Cian.

The timid boy lowered his eyes for a moment before giving a quiet nod.

"...Aine and I can gather the wood."

"There'll be enough."

"And if there isn't," Aine added with a grin, "we'll just make two trips."

Silence settled over the room.

Enna looked from one child to the next.

Three earnest faces stared back at her.

At last, she laughed softly.

"So this was decided before I even woke up?"

"...Maybe."

Aine smiled innocently.

Enna shook her head in surrender.

"I seem to have been outvoted."

She bent down and placed one of the empty buckets into Aedan's hands.

"Very well."

"But if you spill every drop..."

She smiled gently.

"...We'll simply fetch another."

Thus the matter was settled.

Aine and Cian disappeared into the woodland, baskets in hand, their laughter slowly swallowed by the rustling leaves.

Enna and Aedan, meanwhile, took the narrow path leading toward the river.

It was a road they had walked more times than either cared to count.

The morning air still carried the coolness of dawn. Dew clung to the grass beneath their feet, while birds sang freely among the branches overhead. The orphanage is located a bit far from the main village. Therefore, four child have to make do with themselves most of the time.

To Aedan, it was but another ordinary morning.

To me...

It became one worth remembering.

---

At the river:

---

The stream flowed as gently as it always had, its clear waters reflecting the pale morning sky.

Enna knelt upon the bank and lowered the wooden buckets into the current.

When both were filled, she reached for their handles.

Before she could lift them, another hand found one.

"I'll carry this one."

She looked down at Aedan.

"...Are you certain?"

He nodded without hesitation.

"I can do it."

For a brief moment, Enna simply watched him.

Then she let go of the handle.

"Very well."

"But we'll walk slowly."

The bucket proved heavier than it had looked.

Aedan tightened both hands around the handle and took his first careful steps.

One.

Then another.

The water rippled gently within the bucket.

"So far, so good..."

A smile crept across his face.

Then the path dipped ever so slightly.

The water lurched against the rim.

Aedan stumbled.

Cold water splashed across his legs.

"...Ah!"

He hastily steadied the bucket, but every hurried step only sent more water spilling onto the earth.

By the time they reached the shade of an old tree, little more than half remained.

Enna stopped.

"Let's rest a while."

Aedan quietly set the bucket upon the grass.

His clothes clung damply to his knees.

"...I spilled it."

"You did."

"I said I could do it."

"You did."

"...But I couldn't."

Enna sat beneath the old tree and patted the ground beside her.

Aedan lowered the bucket and sat in silence.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

Only the river murmured beside them.

At length, Enna broke the silence.

"...Why are you trying so hard, Aedan?"

The boy stared at the water that remained in the bucket.

"...Because I wanted to help."

"I know."

"But why today?"

He hesitated.

"You always carry both buckets."

"I do."

"They look heavy."

Enna smiled.

"They are."

"...So I thought..."

"If I carried one..."

"...you wouldn't have to."

For a moment, Enna said nothing.

Instead, she looked at the two buckets resting beneath the tree.

"You know..."

"I think today's buckets are lighter."

Aedan looked up, puzzled.

"They're still full."

"They are."

"Then why are they lighter?"

Enna's smile grew a little warmer.

"Because this time..."

"...I had you carrying them with me."

Aedan looked at the bucket in front of him.

Then at the water staining his clothes.

"...I don't understand"

Enna turned to him with the same gentle smile she always wore.

"You don't have to."

She rose to her feet and offered him her hand.

"Come."

"Let's fill it again."

Aedan took her hand without another word.

Together they returned to the river.

The second journey proved little different from the first. Water still found its way over the rim, and the bucket still swayed with every careful step.

Yet somehow...

Aedan found it easier to smile.

---

The years passed as quietly as the seasons themselves.

Spring became summer.

Summer yielded to autumn.

Before anyone had truly noticed...

The little children were children no longer.

Aine, Cian, and Aedan had grown into capable hands around the orphanage. Firewood no longer seemed so heavy, hunting had become a familiar part of their routine, and even the distant woods no longer felt quite as large as they once had.

Yet despite the passing years...

Some things never changed.

Each morning, Enna still rose before the sun.

She still hummed softly while preparing breakfast.

And she still worried over the three of them far more than herself.

---

As autumn settled over the valley once again, signs of the coming Harvest Festival slowly appeared throughout the village.

No grand banners marked the occasion.

Instead, the villagers adorned their homes with carved wooden ornaments, woven wreaths of dried wheat, and strings of polished river shells that chimed gently whenever the wind passed through the streets.

Children gathered fallen leaves to decorate the square, while the scent of fresh bread and roasted game drifted from open kitchens.

It was never a lavish celebration.

Yet every year, the little village welcomed it with the same quiet warmth.

Only a week remained.

---

One evening, after supper, Enna carried the empty dishes outside to wash.

The moment the door slid shut behind her, Aine looked around the table.

"So..."

Aedan tilted his head.

"Doing what?"- Aedan

Aine stared at him.

"A present." 

"For Enna." - Cian

Aedan blinked.

"We've never given her one before." - Aine

"Exactly."

Cian smiled faintly.

"...She's always the one preparing everything for us."

"...Maybe it's our turn."

Aedan looked toward the doorway.

"...What would she even want?"

Aine leaned back in thought.

"I don't know what she wants."

"...But I know what she needs."

She reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

"Every time she cooks..."

"Her hair keeps falling into her face."

"I've seen her fix it a hundred times."

"So..."

"I'm making her a proper hairpin."

---

The others nodded.

"...That sounds like you."

Aine grinned.

"What about you, Cian?"

He hesitated before speaking.

"...Do you remember the stew she talked about?"

"The one she have had when she was a child."

Aedan nodded.

"The one she said she couldn't remember."

"I have checked the book in the library"

"There are an old cookbook. I think I can make some thing similar to her description"

"...I want to make that stew for her."

For a brief moment...

The room fell silent.

Then Aine smiled.

"I think she'd cry."

"...I hope not."

Cian laughed awkwardly.

---

Finally, both of them turned toward Aedan.

"And you?"

He thought for a moment.

"....The village fill with some rumor "

"The blue stones found on the cave."

"They're said to bring good fortune."

Aine raised an eyebrow.

"You believe that?"

Aedan shrugged.

"Not really."

"...But..."

He glanced toward the door where Enna had gone.

"...If there's even a chance..."

"...I'd like her to have a little more luck."

Neither Aine nor Cian laughed.

Instead...

Aine smiled.

"...That's a very Aedan answer."

She stood from her chair.

"Then it's settled."

"A hairpin."

"A soup recipe."

"And a lucky necklace."

"We've only got a week."

"So we'd better get started."

---

The following morning marked the beginning of their little adventure.


---

Cian quietly stepped out from behind his rock and dusted the dirt from his clothes.

"...I hope there's still bread."

"There won't be if Aine gets there first," Aedan answered.

"I heard that!" Aine shouted.

She immediately broke into a run.

Aedan gave chase.

Cian sighed and followed after them at his own careful pace.

The four gathered around the little table, their wooden swords left forgotten by the door

Aedan puffed out his chest.

"The monster won't trouble the village again."

Enna smiled as she placed another bowl upon the table.

"How fortunate."

She paused.

"Now be just as brave against your vegetables."

The little table was filled with laughter.

Looking back upon that afternoon, I cannot think of a day more peaceful than that.
...Or perhaps I can no longer remember it clearly.
Let us simply agree it was a peaceful day.

The days that followed differed little from one another.

Each morning the little household divided its chores as it always had. Aine and Cian would gather fallen branches from the woods, while Enna made her familiar walk to the village well, returning with two heavy buckets balanced across her shoulders.

So it had always been.

Until one morning.

Enna had scarcely reached for the buckets when Aedan spoke.

"Enna."

She looked over.

"I'll come with you today."

She smiled.

"And leave Aine and Cian to gather all the firewood by themselves?"

Before Aedan could answer, Aine folded her arms.

"We talked about it."

Enna blinked.

"You... talked about it?"

Aine nodded matter-of-factly.

"You always carry both buckets."

"...That's your job."

"It doesn't have to be."

Enna looked toward Cian.

The timid boy lowered his eyes for a moment before giving a quiet nod.

"...Aine and I can gather the wood."

"There'll be enough."

"And if there isn't," Aine added with a grin, "we'll just make two trips."

Silence settled over the room.

Enna looked from one child to the next.

Three earnest faces stared back at her.

At last, she laughed softly.

"So this was decided before I even woke up?"

"...Maybe."

Aine smiled innocently.

Enna shook her head in surrender.

"I seem to have been outvoted."

She bent down and placed one of the empty buckets into Aedan's hands.

"Very well."

"But if you spill every drop..."

She smiled gently.

"...We'll simply fetch another."

Thus the matter was settled.

Aine and Cian disappeared into the woodland, baskets in hand, their laughter slowly swallowed by the rustling leaves.

Enna and Aedan, meanwhile, took the narrow path leading toward the river.

It was a road they had walked more times than either cared to count.

The morning air still carried the coolness of dawn. Dew clung to the grass beneath their feet, while birds sang freely among the branches overhead. The orphanage is located a bit far from the main village. Therefore, four child have to make do with themselves most of the time.

To Aedan, it was but another ordinary morning.

To me...

It became one worth remembering.

---

At the river:

---

The stream flowed as gently as it always had, its clear waters reflecting the pale morning sky.

Enna knelt upon the bank and lowered the wooden buckets into the current.

When both were filled, she reached for their handles.

Before she could lift them, another hand found one.

"I'll carry this one."

She looked down at Aedan.

"...Are you certain?"

He nodded without hesitation.

"I can do it."

For a brief moment, Enna simply watched him.

Then she let go of the handle.

"Very well."

"But we'll walk slowly."

The bucket proved heavier than it had looked.

Aedan tightened both hands around the handle and took his first careful steps.

One.

Then another.

The water rippled gently within the bucket.

"So far, so good..."

A smile crept across his face.

Then the path dipped ever so slightly.

The water lurched against the rim.

Aedan stumbled.

Cold water splashed across his legs.

"...Ah!"

He hastily steadied the bucket, but every hurried step only sent more water spilling onto the earth.

By the time they reached the shade of an old tree, little more than half remained.

Enna stopped.

"Let's rest a while."

Aedan quietly set the bucket upon the grass.

His clothes clung damply to his knees.

"...I spilled it."

"You did."

"I said I could do it."

"You did."

"...But I couldn't."

Enna sat beneath the old tree and patted the ground beside her.

Aedan lowered the bucket and sat in silence.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

Only the river murmured beside them.

At length, Enna broke the silence.

"...Why are you trying so hard, Aedan?"

The boy stared at the water that remained in the bucket.

"...Because I wanted to help."

"I know."

"But why today?"

He hesitated.

"You always carry both buckets."

"I do."

"They look heavy."

Enna smiled.

"They are."

"...So I thought..."

"If I carried one..."

"...you wouldn't have to."

For a moment, Enna said nothing.

Instead, she looked at the two buckets resting beneath the tree.

"You know..."

"I think today's buckets are lighter."

Aedan looked up, puzzled.

"They're still full."

"They are."

"Then why are they lighter?"

Enna's smile grew a little warmer.

"Because this time..."

"...I had you carrying them with me."

Aedan looked at the bucket in front of him.

Then at the water staining his clothes.

"...I don't understand"

Enna turned to him with the same gentle smile she always wore.

"You don't have to."

She rose to her feet and offered him her hand.

"Come."

"Let's fill it again."

Aedan took her hand without another word.

Together they returned to the river.

The second journey proved little different from the first. Water still found its way over the rim, and the bucket still swayed with every careful step.

Yet somehow...

Aedan found it easier to smile.

---

The years passed as quietly as the seasons themselves.

Spring became summer.

Summer yielded to autumn.

Before anyone had truly noticed...

The little children were children no longer.

Aine, Cian, and Aedan had grown into capable hands around the orphanage. Firewood no longer seemed so heavy, hunting had become a familiar part of their routine, and even the distant woods no longer felt quite as large as they once had.

Yet despite the passing years...

Some things never changed.

Each morning, Enna still rose before the sun.

She still hummed softly while preparing breakfast.

And she still worried over the three of them far more than herself.

---

As autumn settled over the valley once again, signs of the coming Harvest Festival slowly appeared throughout the village.

No grand banners marked the occasion.

Instead, the villagers adorned their homes with carved wooden ornaments, woven wreaths of dried wheat, and strings of polished river shells that chimed gently whenever the wind passed through the streets.

Children gathered fallen leaves to decorate the square, while the scent of fresh bread and roasted game drifted from open kitchens.

It was never a lavish celebration.

Yet every year, the little village welcomed it with the same quiet warmth.

Only a week remained.

---

One evening, after supper, Enna carried the empty dishes outside to wash.

The moment the door slid shut behind her, Aine looked around the table.

"So..."

Aedan tilted his head.

"Doing what?"- Aedan

Aine stared at him.

"A present." 

"For Enna." - Cian

Aedan blinked.

"We've never given her one before." - Aine

"Exactly."

Cian smiled faintly.

"...She's always the one preparing everything for us."

"...Maybe it's our turn."

Aedan looked toward the doorway.

"...What would she even want?"

Aine leaned back in thought.

"I don't know what she wants."

"...But I know what she needs."

She reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

"Every time she cooks..."

"Her hair keeps falling into her face."

"I've seen her fix it a hundred times."

"So..."

"I'm making her a proper hairpin."

---

The others nodded.

"...That sounds like you."

Aine grinned.

"What about you, Cian?"

He hesitated before speaking.

"...Do you remember the stew she talked about?"

"The one she have had when she was a child."

Aedan nodded.

"The one she said she couldn't remember."

"I have checked the book in the library"

"There are an old cookbook. I think I can make some thing similar to her description"

"...I want to make that stew for her."

For a brief moment...

The room fell silent.

Then Aine smiled.

"I think she'd cry."

"...I hope not."

Cian laughed awkwardly.

---

Finally, both of them turned toward Aedan.

"And you?"

He thought for a moment.

"....The village fill with some rumor "

"The blue stones found on the cave."

"They're said to bring good fortune."

Aine raised an eyebrow.

"You believe that?"

Aedan shrugged.

"Not really."

"...But..."

He glanced toward the door where Enna had gone.

"...If there's even a chance..."

"...I'd like her to have a little more luck."

Neither Aine nor Cian laughed.

Instead...

Aine smiled.

"...That's a very Aedan answer."

She stood from her chair.

"Then it's settled."

"A hairpin."

"A soup recipe."

"And a lucky necklace."

"We've only got a week."

"So we'd better get started."

---

The following morning marked the beginning of their little adventure.

messages.content: How does would you describe this story?

The story is really a quiet exploration of innocent domestic life, focusing on how a small, close-knit family unit navigates routine, responsibility, and profound emotional milestones while being observed by an older generation ("the Olds").

At its heart, it deals with the tension between childhood imagination and settled reality. While the characters—Aedan, Aine, Cian, Enna—have established structured routines through necessary chores like gathering wood or fetching water, moments of intense imaginative play (like a boy charging an oak tree) reveal the powerful inner lives that drive them.

The emotional core revolves around mutual support and preparation for transition. The group is deeply focused on nurturing each other's well-being, particularly concerning Enna. This sense of shared purpose builds toward a planned celebration or rite of passage. Ultimately, the story captures the anticipatory quiet—a countdown to an Autumn Harvest Festival marked by three specific acts of care: the preparation of a lucky necklace, a special stew recipe, and a hairpin that signals the beginning of their little adventure.
